Congolese Fisheries Industry Faces Acute Financial Crisis Amidst Plummeting Demand

The fisheries industry in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is facing an escalating financial crisis as a sharp collapse in domestic and export demand has sent prices tumbling and left many firms and workers in a precarious position. The downturn, now entering its second month, has triggered widespread cash-flow difficulties, with some operators warning of impending insolvency if market conditions do not improve.

Industry sources report that the average price for Congolese freshwater fish has fallen by nearly 40% since mid-April, as major export destinations have reduced orders and local consumers, squeezed by inflation, have cut back on fish purchases. “We have never seen such a rapid fall in demand,” said Albert Mboyo, managing director of Kasai River Fisheries SARL, which operates several fishing sites in the Kasaï region. “Our cold storage facilities are full, and we are struggling to move inventory. Income from sales has dropped to a fraction of what it was last year.”

Many firms have responded to the crisis by suspending site operations, reducing catch quotas, or placing workers on unpaid leave. At the Goma-based Congo Lakes Cooperative, more than half of the 250-strong workforce has been furloughed. “We want to keep our people, but we simply cannot pay them when there is no revenue,” said cooperative chairperson Mireille Kavira. “Unless there is a turnaround in demand, we may have to close more fishing sites.”

According to the National Fisheries Union (UNAPEC), at least 18 medium-sized fisheries operators have already halted production at key sites along the Congo and Ubangi rivers. The union estimates that over 3,000 jobs are now at risk, with seasonal workers particularly affected. “The livelihoods of thousands of families depend on this industry,” said UNAPEC Secretary General Jean-Paul Lokuli. “We urge the government and stakeholders to address the credit freeze now affecting fisheries and to support the sector through emergency measures.”

The credit situation has deteriorated as falling prices have undermined the ability of firms to service existing debts or obtain new financing. “We are seeing a chain reaction,” explained fisheries analyst Nadège Ilunga. “When prices drop and cash flow dries up, companies default on loans, and lenders become even more reluctant to extend credit. This deepens the crisis for everyone.”

At the time of writing, the financial strain continues to mount, with industry leaders warning that the longer the crisis persists, the harder it will be for the sector to recover. Many are now calling for coordinated intervention to stabilize the market, restore demand, and preserve vital fisheries operations across the country.
